Where the Shadow Leans

by starlite_starbrite

Summary

A Vampire King × Elven Prince AU.

Every elf knows never to touch a vampire. Every vampire knows that elven blood is lethal.

The Sovereign of the Coast takes the sun prince of Aloria as his hostage, and then as his.

Anyone who tries to take him back will learn why the shadows lean away from Arian Conti, and towards nothing else but Caleb.

Notes

My deepest thanks to Emo Universe, who created the most perfect male lead in Caleb Whitmore, matched only by his devoted future husband, Arian Conti.

Caleb, I love you. You deserve nothing but goodness, perfection, and Arian Conti.

A little background, for the curious. I've been building this world for many, many years, inspired by the worlds of Robert Jordan, Brandon Sanderson and J.R.R. Tolkien. The realms, the Accord, the crystals and the Long Eclipse have lived in my notebooks all this while, waiting for the right characters. Every choice I tried felt wrong, and I never managed to create any original characters who satisfied me enough to write a story about. And then along came Caleb and Arian, and FINALLY, at long last, this world had its main characters, and a story.

While I write purely for my own self-indulgence, I am very grateful to everyone reading.

A short guide to the world - Each realm draws on the culture and geography of a real-world country.

The realms

  • Aloria, the Solar Dominion (elves, loosely Britain) - Caleb's home. Great Aether-crystals on the spires of the Citadel keep it noon around the clock, so an elf who wants a night has to close the shutters. The Radiant Guard, the temple-schools of the Harp Vales and the Highland March are all here.
  • Vesperia, the Umbral Syndicate (vampires, loosely Italy) - Arian's realm, under volcanic ash and a violet twilight that never lifts. He rules from Castel Nerezza on the Obsidian Coast, and the great houses sit on the Council of Nine. Vampires are a quiet, secretive people, even by the standards of the other realms.
  • The Court of Lys (fae, loosely France) - the fae cannot lie, so they make good diplomats and witnesses, and nobody sensible tells them a secret. Their broadsheet, the Lantern of Lutèce, turns up everywhere.
  • The Deep Holds (dwarves, loosely Austria, Germany and Switzerland) - engineers and bankers. Their vault-city, Durnhollow, takes no sides.
  • Lowmere (gnomes, the Low Countries) runs the world's trade. Thalassa (merfolk, Greece) has the seas and the harbour of Nauplion, and the Jötun North (giants, Scandinavia) mostly stays out of it.
  • Lycans don't have a realm of their own. Their hill towns are in the Wildmarch, high in the Eclipse Marches, but they live all over and serve in both courts. Unlike elves and vampires, who stop ageing once they reach their prime, they age, and they turn grey early (like us humans!!!)
  • Hedge-witches belong to no realm and no court. They keep to the back streets of other people's cities, and grow and brew the things that great houses would rather not be seen buying.
  • The Eclipse Marches are the neutral mountains in between, where day and night still behave normally.
See the end of the work for more notes

Chapter 1: Prologue - The Long Eclipse

Every child from the Jötun North to the shores of the Middle Sea knows how the story ends. Almost no one knows how it began.

— A History of the Long Eclipse, by Aurèle Vasseur, historian to the Court of Lys

* * *

On the day the sun went out, Livia Conti walked beneath the open sky at last, and she did not look up once.

She had meant to. All her long life she had heard the elders describe it, the day that came but once in twenty years, when the great light faltered and the children of the Umbral houses might stand in the world as other people stood in it. Every twenty years the Sovereign’s delegation had gone to meet it, and every twenty years she had stayed behind to keep the Sanctuary. This time the Sovereign had brought his boy, and asked her to come too. As a girl she had imagined that she would spend it with her face turned upward like a flower. Instead she spent it with her face to the ground, reading the ruins of Old Meridian for the Sovereign’s son.

The Summit had come apart an hour after noon.

When the first cry rang out, Livia had been in the great silk tent where the Vesperian delegation received its guests, pouring blood-wine for a dwarven envoy who had talked of nothing but tariffs since the eclipse began. A second cry followed, and then the high, bright scream of silver leaving a sheath. By the time she reached the fountain court the Sovereign lay on the flagstones with three blades in him, his guards dead around him. The men who had done it had vanished into the mist. Before that night was out, her husband Enzo would swear that he knew whose men they were. He would swear it for twenty years, but never once be able to prove it.

Enzo had been kneeling in the blood. He looked up at her with a face she had never seen him wear and said one word.

Where?

The boy. He had been at his father’s side not a quarter of an hour since, bored and scowling in his first formal coat, twelve years old and furious at being made to stand still.

Now he was nowhere to be found.

* * *

Enzo had the delegation to hold and the Council to face and a dead Sovereign to keep from becoming a dead dynasty, and so it was Livia who went into the ruins.

Old Meridian had been a city once, before the realms were sundered, and it had never quite agreed to stop being one. Its streets still ran where they had always run, paved in a white stone the centuries had worn to the colour of old teeth. Its arches still stood, though nothing passed beneath them now but fog. The mist of the Marches lay over all of it, thick and cool and faintly luminous, and on this day of all days it glowed with a light that belonged to no hour at all.

The sun had become a black coin rimmed with white fire. Everything beneath it had turned the colour of a pearl held up to a candle. The elves in their silk tents across the valley had gone quiet as their great crystals dimmed, and for this one day the crystals’ glare could not reach her. The whole valley lay in one shadow, so there was none to hide in and nothing to burn her.

She had never been so frightened.

He was bleeding. That much she knew within a hundred paces of the fountain court, and she knew it as any mother knows her own child’s cry through a wall. She had not borne him. She had held him all the same, the night his mother died giving him to the world, and she had held him ever since, most of all on the nights he was too proud to ask. She would have known his blood in a sea of it.

It was on the stones of a narrow street that ran uphill from the old market, and then on the base of a broken column where he must have leaned, and then on a doorframe, a smear the size of a child’s palm, and her own hands shook so badly she had to close them.

There was sun-forged silver in it. She could smell it, bright and sour, under the iron. A blade forged under Aloria’s noon leaves a wound that does not close. She had seen grown men of the Umbral houses die of such a cut in the time it took to call a physician, and he was twelve.

She ran.

* * *

The trail ended at a glasshouse.

It stood at the top of the hill, on the edge of what had once been a garden and was now only a wilderness of briars. It must have been beautiful when the city was young. Its ribs were iron, fine as the bones of a bird, and they rose into a dome that had once been all glass. Most of the panes were gone now. Those that remained were clouded and cracked and hung at angles, and the mist drifted in and out through the gaps like a tenant.

The door stood open. There was blood on the threshold.

Livia went in.

It was warmer inside, and that was wrong. The air under that broken dome was soft and still and faintly golden, a summer afternoon someone had left there and forgotten, and the clouded panes that still clung to the ribs were warm as new bread, under a sun that had given no warmth since noon. The briars grew thinner here. Among them, pale against the dark soil, a few old rose bushes had put out new leaves, tender and absurd, the only living green she had seen in the whole of Old Meridian.

He was lying in the middle of them.

She was on her knees beside him before she knew she had crossed the floor. He lay on his side in the soft earth with his knees drawn up, as he had slept when he was little, and his first formal coat was black and wet and torn open at the side where the blade had gone in. There was so much blood around him that the soil had turned to mud.

She pulled the torn coat aside, dreading what she would find, and found nothing. The wound was closed. Where the silver had gone in there was only smooth skin and a thin seam of gold light that faded as she watched, like the last line of a sunset going under the sea.

She stared at it. No physician of the Umbral houses could close such a wound, and no magic she had ever heard of could do it.

Then she saw the cloak.

It was wrapped around his shoulders and tucked beneath his chin with tender care, and it was not his. It was a child’s cloak, too small for him, of pale grey wool so fine it was nearly silk, and it was stitched all through with silver thread that caught the light of the eclipse and held it. At the collar, worked in gold, was a sunburst.

Livia knew that sunburst. It was known in every realm under the sun.

It was the crest of the Solar House.

* * *

She had scarcely taken it in when she heard the footsteps.

They were light and quick and receding. She turned her head, and through the broken glass on the far side of the dome she saw a figure running away from her into the mist.

It was a child, younger than her boy, running with his arms pumping and his elbows out, as children run before anyone has taught them to run like gentlemen. His hair was a warm dark brown, but a faint golden glow clung about him all the same, and it moved through the mist like a lamp being carried away. He ran down the hill towards the elven tents, where she could hear voices now, many voices, calling a name the mist would not let her catch.

At the edge of the briars he stopped, and looked back.

She could not see his face. He was too far away, and the mist was too thick. She saw only that he stood a moment, turned towards the glasshouse, unwilling to go until he was sure someone had found her boy. Then the voices called again, closer, and he turned and ran, and the mist closed over him.

It never occurred to her to follow. She had her boy.

* * *

He woke as she was lifting him.

His eyes opened, dark and unfocused, and his hand came up and closed hard on the cloak at his throat, in case she meant to take it.

“Hush,” she murmured. “Hush, tesoro. It is Zia. I have you.”

He looked at her for a long moment. Then his gaze went past her, over her shoulder, to the empty place among the roses where he had lain.

“He was here.”

“Who was here?”

“He was warm.” His voice was thin as thread. His hand did not let go of the cloak. “He wasn’t afraid of me. He should have been afraid of me, Zia, I told him what I was, and he wasn’t, he just put his hands on the hurt and it got warm and he stayed —” He stopped. His breath caught. “Where did he go?”

“Home,” said Livia, because she did not know what else to say.

The boy closed his eyes.

She carried him out of the glasshouse and down the long white streets of Old Meridian, under the black sun, with his head against her shoulder and the little grey cloak still clutched at his throat. He said nothing more, and she thought he had gone back to sleep.

Halfway down the hill, he whispered into her collar, “Help me find him.”

She had no answer to give him.

* * *

The sun returned. It came back first as a thread of white fire along the rim of the black coin, and the thread swelled to a sickle and the sickle to a blaze, and every shadow in Old Meridian drew itself back out of the pearl and lay down again where it belonged. The elves went home to their light. In the Vesperian tent Enzo sat for an hour with his head in his hands, and then he rose, because a dynasty does not wait upon grief.

Livia put the boy to bed herself. She sat beside him in the dark, as she had sat on a thousand nights before, and rested her hand upon his chest to feel him breathe.

Beneath her palm, faint and slow and impossible, his heart was beating.

The children of the Umbral houses have no heartbeat, and every one of them knows it. It is the first thing they are taught about themselves.

Livia sat motionless in the dark for a long time, with her hand over the heart of a child who had been healed by the Solar House, and she told no one. She did not tell Enzo, or the Council, or, for many years, the boy himself.

When at last he let go of the little silver cloak, she folded it with great care and put it away somewhere safe. Then, in the quietest way she knew, she began to help him look.

Chapter 2: Chapter One - The Ash of the Solar Crest

Where the blood of an Umbral house is shed upon Umbral ground by a hand of the Solar House, the wronged may claim the debt in blood, or in a hostage of equal rank. The hostage passes wholly into the keeping of the wronged, and his own house shall have no further claim upon him.

— The Twilight Accord, Article Nine (translated from the Lyssois)

* * *

Caleb woke to the taste of ash.

It was the stale, powdery taste of a hearth no one had swept in centuries, and it settled on his tongue like the dust of an old library. He lay still and allowed the world to arrange itself about him by degrees. First came the low hum of light-engines beneath the deck, then the ache behind his eyes, then the cool silk of a chaise beneath his cheek. His last clear memory was a glass of Citadel white, pressed into his hand by his mother’s chamberlain, and the chamberlain’s face as he drank, composed into a blankness so courteous that it ought to have warned him.

Ah, he thought. So that is how we are to do it.

He sat up. The sky-yacht’s cabin was all pale ashwood and polished silver, with the royal sunburst worked into every panel and fitting lest he forget whose property he was. The sunbursts had been made to drink the Citadel’s noon and give it back, and out here, with nothing to drink, every one of them had faded to the tired yellow of a pear left too long in the bowl. Beyond the porthole there was no sky at all, only a ceiling of volcanic cloud rolling over itself like a disgruntled sea, and beneath it a coastline of black stone that fell away into canyons so deep their floors were lost to sight, pricked here and there with violet light like embers in a banked fire.

The Obsidian Coast. He had seen it on maps his whole life, inked in black along the bottom edge of the known world beneath a line of immaculate Alorian script. Here the light does not reach.

On the cabin’s display panel, a holographic broadsheet turned in slow, gilded circles. His own face smiled out of it, borrowed from last season’s portrait, the one in which the painter had so generously improved upon his jaw. Beneath it ran a royal decree in his father’s florid hand. His Royal Highness Prince Caleb has departed upon a sacred and solitary pilgrimage to the outer temples. The Crown asks that his privacy be respected in this season of reflection.

He read it twice. Then he laughed, once, and it did not come out right.

“A season of reflection,” he announced to the empty cabin. “How very poetic of them. And I suppose they are not wrong about the solitude, at least.”

His father had come to his rooms the evening before, which his father never did. The King had stood by the window with his back to the room and said that Caleb’s signet ring had been found at a vineyard in the Marches, among the dead. Caleb had waited for the rest of the sentence. There had been no rest of the sentence. There had only been the chamberlain, and the wine.

His signet. He had lent it to his brother Andrew weeks ago, laughing, because Andrew had asked and Caleb had never refused Andrew anything. Andrew would have given it back. Andrew must have given it back, and Caleb had simply misplaced it, the way he misplaced gloves and hours and the names of minor ambassadors.

He set the thought aside like a letter in a familiar hand, and did not open it.

He rose and straightened the silver-threaded lapels of his coat. He saw that his hands were not steady, and folded them behind his back until they were, and went to the door.

Paul Walker was standing outside it, as he had stood outside every door Caleb had slept behind since Caleb was fourteen. The Accord allowed a hostage one sworn attendant, and someone had seen to it that the attendant was Paul. Caleb smiled at him with the whole of his face, as a traveller smiles at the first lit window on a long road home.

Paul stared at the floor.

* * *

They brought the yacht down into a courtyard of black stone cut into the mountain’s flank, and when the hatch folded open the Coast’s twilight came in to meet him. It was violet at the edges and ash-dark at the heart, and it neither brightened nor deepened but only hung over everything, so that the gold of the yacht’s lamps spilling across the flagstones behind him looked suddenly gaudy, like a kingfisher that has blundered into a rookery. The air pressed close and heavy. It smelled of volcanic stone and crushed velvet and, beneath both, the faint copper of very old blood.

The hall into which they delivered him had been carved rather than built. Its walls rose in ridged black columns of volcanic glass that caught what little light there was and swallowed it. Crystal lamps hung on chains from a height he could not see, each burning a low and bruised violet, enough to see by and nowhere near enough to feel. After twenty-eight years beneath the Citadel’s eternal noon, Caleb’s skin took the gloom for cold, and he wanted, with undignified urgency, to chafe his arms.

He kept them where they were. He was a prince of the Solar House, and there was an audience.

A lycan stood sentinel by the doors, Marches-born by the look of him, grey-flecked and monumental, his Conti black stretched over a body that plainly would rather have gone without it. His nostrils flared as Caleb passed. Then they flared again at Paul, who had followed two paces behind, and the rumble that rose in the sentinel’s chest had nothing welcoming in it. A lycan in Alorian livery was evidently a thing to be despised on this coast.

Against the far wall a fae in a coat of iridescent feathers sat perched on the arm of a chair, walking a thin copper coin across her knuckles. It chimed, softly and sweetly, each time it turned. Beside her stood a vampire in dove grey, with a face that looked no older than thirty and eyes that looked a great deal older. He wore the pained, upright bearing Caleb knew from every minister who had ever lost an argument with his father.

And at the far end of the hall, behind a desk of black stone, someone sat in the dark.

Caleb could not see him. He could feel him, as one feels the edge of a cliff in darkness. The Star-Grace beneath his skin, that quiet golden thread of healing magic he had carried since birth, drew in on itself like a flower closing in sudden shade. He had heard the stories every Alorian child heard, of the pull the old vampire bloodlines exerted, of grown knights swooning in the presence of a Sovereign. What he felt was the cold and the drop and the dark, and nothing in the least like swooning.

He reminded himself that every creature in the room could hear his heart, which was beating like a finch against the bars of a gilded cage, and there was nothing to be done about that. There was a great deal to be done about his face.

He allowed his gaze to travel the hall, from the columns to the chains to the unrelieved dark, and let his face settle into polite, well-bred suffering, as if a friend were showing him round some regrettable renovations.

“How perfectly atmospheric,” he said, and the hall gave his voice back to him, silken and unhurried. “I confess myself curious. Is the darkness an aesthetic conviction, or has someone in this household forgotten to pay the chandler? I ask only because I should hate to walk into a pillar and provoke a diplomatic incident.” Then, as if it had only that moment occurred to him, he added, “Another diplomatic incident, I should say.”

The fae’s coin stopped mid-turn. The sentinel made a sound suspiciously like a laugh, and hastily turned it into a cough. The grey-suited vampire shut his eyes and appeared to pray for patience to a god he had stopped believing in some centuries ago.

From the far end of the hall came the scrape of a chair.

* * *

Arian Conti was younger than Caleb had expected.

The fae broadsheets that fluttered through the Citadel’s lower markets, the scandalous ones that no prince of the Solar House was permitted to read and that Caleb devoured with his breakfast, called him the Sovereign of Vesperia, the Youngest Don, the Knife of the Obsidian Coast. Youngest or not, he was a vampire, and Caleb had furnished his imagination with someone ancient, gaunt and faintly mildewed. The man who came out of the dark looked scarcely older than Caleb himself.

He resolved from the gloom like ink running backwards into water. He was a full head taller than Caleb, lean and broad through the shoulders, and he wore a shirt of heavy black silk buttoned to the throat without a crease anywhere on it. His hair was black, worn a little long and swept back from his brow, save for a single lock that had escaped across his forehead. Three rings of old, heavy gold sat on his right hand, one of them set with a stone so black it resembled a void.

Every child in Aloria was told that the Umbral houses were beautiful, in the same breath and the same tone in which they were told that nightshade was pretty. Caleb had grown up among beauty, and was generally held to be a rather dazzling example of it himself, though he had always privately suspected that people mistook his good humour for good looks. Elven beauty was a warm thing, lit from within, the kind that flushed and laughed and turned its face towards the sun. This was the other kind. It was the beauty of marble in a cold gallery, or of a blade laid out on velvet, flawless and unapproachable. Arian’s face was all severe, clean angles, with a jaw that might have been cut from the obsidian around him and cheekbones a court painter would have wept to be allowed near. His eyes were so dark there was no telling iris from pupil. It was, Caleb thought with considerable annoyance, a face entirely wasted on its owner, who plainly neither knew what he had nor cared.

The candles in their iron sconces guttered as he passed, each flame shrinking down into its wick like a child ducking under the bedclothes at a tread on the stair, and the air cooled a degree at a time.

He crossed the hall without hurrying, as a tide comes in, and stopped an arm’s length away. It was near enough that Caleb had to tip his head back to meet Arian’s eyes, and Caleb resented that immediately and with his whole heart.

And now, at last, Caleb felt what the stories spoke of. It was a pull, low and steady and without malice, like the tug of deep water at the end of a pier, or a compass needle turning helplessly to the north. Some quiet, treacherous part of him wanted to take one step nearer. He did not. He set his heels into the black stone as his sister Matilda had taught him to set them against a charge, and stayed where he was, and hoped devoutly that it did not show.

People generally looked at Caleb’s hair, or his famous smile, or the headlines that trailed behind him like a train. Arian studied his face the way a scholar studies a difficult text. His gaze went down to Caleb’s hands, still clasped behind his back, and then to the faint shimmer along his jaw where the Star-Grace lay nearest the skin. Caleb knew with a jolt that the light there was dimmer than it had been that morning.

If Arian’s face had an opinion on the matter, it kept it. Yet under that dark regard the faint gold along Caleb’s jaw brightened for a moment, as a candle does when a door opens somewhere far down a passage, and then lay quiet again.

“Your Royal Highness.” The voice was low and even, with the roll of the Coast running under the Alorian vowels like a current under still water.

“Sovereign.” Caleb inclined his head as far as protocol required for a foreign head of state, and not one hair further. “I would offer you my hand, but I have been reliably informed that your people bite.”

“Only when invited.”

He said it so flatly that a full second passed before Caleb understood it had been a joke. By then Arian had moved on.

“You know why you are here.”

“I have formed a working hypothesis.” Caleb let the words take their time. “It concerns my family, a vineyard I have never set foot in, and a considerable number of people who would very much like me to stop asking questions. Oh, and a glass of wine, drugged, which I consider the greatest crime of the lot, since it was an exceptional vintage and deserved a far kinder end.”

He had meant it lightly. It emerged with rather more feeling than he had intended, and Arian’s eyes dropped for an instant to his throat. To his pulse, Caleb understood, and his face went hot, for naturally his own pulse was reading out his every feeling to the room, like a herald at a banquet announcing guests nobody had invited.

“I know you were not at the vineyard.”

Caleb opened his mouth, found nothing in it, and closed it again.

He had spent the rest of that flight bracing for this room, and had prepared answers for accusation and for contempt, for a cell, a chain, a slow and inventive death, and not a single word for being believed.

“You know,” he repeated.

“Yes.”

“Then —” His voice had started to climb. He caught it and hauled it back down. “Then with the greatest respect, Sovereign, what in the Sun’s holy name am I doing here?”

Arian regarded him for a long moment.

“They sent you,” he answered, and seemed to consider that a full explanation.

The grey-suited vampire shifted his weight. Arian did not look at him.

“Your Royal Seal.” Arian held out his hand.

* * *

Caleb’s fingers went to his breast pocket before he realised they were moving.

The seal had lived there since his coming-of-age, a medallion of sun-forged silver the size of his palm, with the crest of the Solar House on one face and his own name on the other. It was always warm to the touch, as a sleeping animal is warm. It was his passport and his immunity and his signature. With it he could walk into any embassy of the Dominion and be known. Without it he was a beautifully dressed elf with no name at all.

He drew it out reluctantly. It lay in his palm, glowing a soft and living gold, the brightest thing in the hall.

“Do try not to scratch it. The scribes of the Citadel are glacial in the matter of replacements. I should be waiting six months at the very least, in queues I can only describe as unspeakable.”

Across the hall, the fae’s copper coin began to sing, a thin, high, insistent note that did not stop, like a wet fingertip drawn around the rim of a glass. The fae abandoned her idle play and held the coin up between two fingers, head tilted, delighted.

“Oh, it’s singing, Sovereign.” She savoured the words like sugared almonds. “And ever so loudly.”

Caleb glanced at her and back down at the seal. The seal was worth a king’s ransom, or at any rate a prince’s. Perhaps her coin had an eye for valuables. He let it fall into Arian’s waiting palm.

Arian’s fingers closed over it.

For a moment nothing happened. Then the air around his fist changed. It thickened and darkened, and every shadow in the hall leaned in towards him to see. The seal’s light flared gold between his knuckles, bright enough that Caleb had to narrow his eyes, and there came from it a sound he would remember long afterwards, a thin and rising keen, like a living thing in terror.

Then the keening stopped, and the light died with it.

Arian opened his hand. What was left of the seal ran from between his fingers in a slow, bright thread and pattered onto the black floor, where it hissed and cooled and dulled to the colour of a winter sky. The palm beneath was red and blistered, as if he had closed his hand on a burning coal, and he did not so much as glance at it. The fae’s coin fell silent in the middle of its note.

Caleb looked down at the grey pool at his feet.

He had known since he woke that he was not going home. The drugged wine, the decree, the crew who would not meet his eye, and Paul. Yet he had known it only as a child knows the ending of a tale before the last page is turned, and now he had watched the last thing in the world that bore his name run molten across a stranger’s floor, and his heart turned over painfully in the silence of that hall.

He could not look at Arian yet. His eyes went to the fae instead, and then to the grey-suited vampire, who had barely glanced at Caleb until now. The vampire was staring at him openly, at Caleb’s face and hands and the last of the gold along his jaw, and the colour had drained from his own cheeks.

“Well,” Caleb said to the floor, when he trusted his voice to hold. “Eleven years of absolute sovereignty, Don Conti, and it seems no one has ever shown you how a seal is used. It is the wax one is meant to melt, you understand, not the seal itself. How delightfully unrefined of you.”

* * *

“Enzo.”

The grey-suited vampire came forward. He carried a casket of dark oiled wood, carved with the square, angular runes Caleb knew from the dwarven vault-banks of the Marches, and he opened it with a reluctance so plain it might have been a third person in the conversation.

“Sovereign.” Enzo kept his voice low. “Once more, I beg you. Consider what that ring will say to every house on the Coast —”

“I have considered it.”

Enzo’s jaw set. He held the casket out at the full length of his arm and said nothing more.

From it Arian lifted a ring. It was a plain band of black iron, heavier than it had any right to look, with a single line of dwarven runes cut around its face. A tiny closed crescent was engraved into the iron, the crest of House Conti, and beside it sat an empty setting where a stone was meant to go and had not yet arrived. To Caleb’s eye it was a thing fit for a favourite hunting hound.

“Your hand.”

“I find I am rather attached to it.”

Arian waited. It became clear that he was prepared to wait for the rest of the night, and quite possibly the century.

Caleb held out his left hand, palm down, as he might to a courtier he disliked who was angling to kiss it.

Arian took his wrist.

His grip was cool. Caleb had expected cold, and it was only cool, like stone that has lain a long while in shade. He turned Caleb’s hand over with a care that was almost clinical and slid the iron band onto his ring finger. It was too large. Then the runes met his skin and it was not. A thread of light ran once around them, quick as a minnow turning in a shallow stream, and the metal drew in, snug and painless, until it sat on his finger as if forged for no other hand.

And under Arian’s fingers, where they rested against the inside of his wrist, Caleb felt a pulse.

The beat was faint and slow, and unmistakable. He had been taught to heal by counting heartbeats before he had been taught to read. He went still.

Vampires had no pulse. It was the second thing the temple tutors taught about them, straight after they burn in the light. Their hearts do not beat.

It must be his own, then. His own blood, racing and loud, coming back to him through the contact. That was all it could be.

Arian let go, and the feeling went with him.

“Wear it. Do not take it off.”

Caleb looked at the black iron on his finger, at the Conti crest and the empty setting, and humiliation arrived all at once, scalding and complete. The seal of his own house was slag on the floor, and in its place he had been given a collar. Property, duly marked.

“How exceedingly thoughtful.” He was rather proud of how bored he sounded. “Is there to be a matching lead, or shall I expect that with the morning post?”

Nobody laughed this time. The sentinel at the door was staring at the ring. So was the fae, who had gone motionless on the arm of her chair with her lips parted, like someone who had just been handed the finest secret of her long, long life. Enzo had turned his face away altogether.

Caleb saw none of it. He was looking at Arian, and Arian was looking back at him with the same unfathomable stillness.

“You will have rooms in the east wing. Ask for whatever you require. You will not leave the fortress.”

“And should I try?”

“You will not get far.”

“How reassuring. Tell me, Sovereign, is that meant as concern for my welfare, or as a threat?”

Arian looked at him a moment longer.

“Yes,” he said, and turned away.

* * *

The sentinel walked him out, with Paul silent at his back. Caleb went with his chin up and his shoulders square, just as Matilda had drilled into him on a hundred mornings in the practice yard, and his left hand closed into a fist at his side, the iron on it warm now and heavy.

At the threshold he heard Arian speak behind him, low, to Enzo, in a voice not meant to carry. But the Solar House had always bred for keen ears.

“— to the vault-masons at Durnhollow. Tonight. Tell them I require glass.”

“Glass, Sovereign?”

“Tonight, Zio.”

The great doors swung shut on the rest.

Caleb walked the long black corridor to the east wing, counting the violet lamps as he passed beneath them. At the third he held his hand up to the glass, out of pure stubbornness, and it gave him about as much warmth as a lamp painted in the margin of a book. He counted them so that he would not think about the pulse under Arian’s fingers, or the way Arian had looked at his hands, or the fact that the Sovereign of Vesperia believed him innocent and had kept him anyway, or the signet he had lent his brother weeks ago, laughing.

He thought instead about the queue at the Citadel’s seal office, which wound three times around the Hall of Petitions and moved at the pace of a tortoise in mourning, and how he would never again have to stand in it. Somewhere between the eleventh lamp and the twelfth, he caught himself laughing, quietly and not quite steadily. The sentinel kept his eyes ahead. Paul, at his back, said nothing.

* * *

Behind him, in the emptied hall, the shadows that had leaned in to watch drew back one by one and went home to the columns, and the Sovereign of Vesperia stood over a pool of cooling silver with his burned hand open at his side, and did not move for a long time.

Chapter 3: Chapter Two - A Garden Beneath the Mountain

The afflicted will sleep long and wake unrested. The cold settles in the hands first, then in the heart, which forgets its measure. Of those taken beyond the reach of the sun, none has been known to live past the tenth week.

— Of the Solar Blight, from the physicians’ primer of the Harp Vales

* * *

On the first day, Caleb asked for books.

He did it chiefly to find out what would happen. He wrote the request out in his most exquisite hand on a sheet of the heavy black paper he found in the escritoire and left it on the silver tray beside the untouched remains of his supper, fully expecting it to be ignored, or mocked, or burned. By the following evening there were forty-three volumes stacked on the table by the window. There was Alorian poetry and Vesperian history, a treatise on dwarven bond-law, three novels of such spectacular vulgarity that he read two of them in one sitting, and a slim, water-stained primer on the healing arts that came unasked and that no one would explain.

On the fourth day, as an experiment, he asked for a harpsichord.

It arrived on the sixth, carried up the stair by four grunting lycans. It was lacquered black and gold, old and fine and slightly out of tune, and he spent a contented afternoon tuning it himself.

On the ninth day he asked for Alorian white tea, which was not exported, and it came on the tenth. On the eleventh, out of pure mischief, he asked for every fae broadsheet printed in the past month, and those came too, the pages still smelling of the Marches. His own face stared up from a good third of them beneath headlines of mounting hysteria. THE PILGRIM PRINCE: WHERE IS CALEB? SOLAR HOUSE SILENT ON YOUNGEST SON. And on the most recent, in a crimson ink that fairly shrieked off the page, TRAITOR PRINCE? Palace Sources Hint at Darker Truth.

He read that one three times. Then he fed it, neatly, to the candle.

Ask for whatever you require, the Sovereign had said, and he had meant it with a thoroughness Caleb found more unsettling than cruelty. Cruelty he would have understood. One could brace against it, and quip at it, and endure. Here every door in the east wing stood unlocked save the one that led out of it, every request was granted save the one he did not trouble to make, and the man who had melted his seal on the floor had not come to see him once in three weeks.

Caleb told himself he was relieved.

* * *

The food came three times a day, and it came with Vesna.

She was a lycan woman of perhaps fifty, broad and brown-armed and smelling of woodsmoke and bread, with a voice that could have called a pack home across a valley. She had appeared on his first morning with a tray of Alorian scones and set it down with the air of someone presenting evidence at a trial.

They were a disaster. They were dense as masonry, scorched on one side and raw on the other, and whoever had written the recipe out for her had plainly never met a scone in his life. Caleb ate every one of them, with butter and a great deal of praise, while Vesna stood over him with her arms folded and watched him do it. On the second morning the scones were merely bad. By the second week they were all but good, and Vesna had begun to call him malyshka, which he gathered meant something like little one, and which no one had called him since he was six.

He asked her how a lycan came to be cooking in a vampire’s fortress. She said the Sovereign had asked her, and that was all she would say, and she said it with a look that closed the subject like a door.

Paul was a different matter. Paul slept across the threshold of Caleb’s bedchamber every night, as he always had, and in three weeks he had said perhaps forty words. Caleb tried everything. He asked after Paul’s mother and sisters in the Highland March, and offered him the vulgar novels. He played the harpsichord badly on purpose, which had always made Paul laugh. Paul thanked him, and looked resolutely at the floor, and went back to the door.

Caleb put it down to shame. It must be hard, for a lycan whose family had kept faith with the Solar House for six generations, to watch the Solar House hand its youngest son to Vesperia. He resolved to be kinder to him, and was.

* * *

The chambers themselves were a study in magnificent melancholy. Tall windows of smoked glass looked out over the jagged black valleys of the Coast, where the twilight never deepened into night or lightened into day but only hung there, violet and charcoal, like a held breath. Hangings of velvet the colour of a bruised plum swallowed what little the candles gave. The bed was a vast, brooding thing of carved ebony, its posts twined with nightshade and serpents, and on the first night Caleb had lain in it and thought, with great clarity, that it resembled nothing so much as a comfortable sarcophagus.

By the third week he no longer thought anything when he lay down in it. He simply slept, and that was how he knew that something was wrong.

He had been trained, as all the children of the Solar House were trained, in the healing arts. Star-Grace was the gift of their blood, and the temple physicians of the Harp Vales had spent a decade of his childhood drilling him in its uses, in the counting of pulses and the reading of breath and the patient, unsentimental study of a body’s betrayals. So when, in the second week, the shimmer on his skin faded from gold to silver and from silver to a flat, chalky pallor, Caleb turned that study on himself. He marked the chill that had settled in his fingertips and stayed there however close he held them to the fire. He counted the fourteen hours of sleep that rested him not at all, and felt the dull weight gather in the tips of his ears. And he listened, at the end of each day, to his heart beginning to stumble over its own rhythm like a dancer who has been too long on the floor.

The primer called it the Solar Blight, and it was plain about its course. Alorians taken beyond the reach of the sun, it observed with scholarly serenity, survived between six and ten weeks.

He found the passage in the water-stained primer that no one would explain, on the evening of the nineteenth day. He closed the book and set it down on the table with great care. Then he went and sat at the harpsichord for a long while, and did not play.

On the twenty-first day, he dressed.

It took more effort than it once had, and he had begun to allow an hour for it. But he dressed with scrupulous care all the same, in a coat of dove-grey silk with silver frogging, a waistcoat embroidered with white stars, and cuffs of Alorian lace so fine they might have been spun by spiders with ambition. There was no one to dress for. He dressed because a prince of the Solar House did not greet his own death in a dressing gown, and because every morning he managed it was a morning on which he had not yet begun to die in earnest.

He was sitting on the chaise by the window, smoothing the lace at his wrists, when the door opened.

* * *

Arian Conti stood on the threshold.

He wore a high-collared coat of black silk that drank the candlelight instead of returning it, and the three heavy rings, and the stillness Caleb remembered from the hall. He offered no greeting. His gaze moved over the room, over the stacked books and the harpsichord and the curl of ash in the candle dish, and came to rest on Caleb.

Caleb saw Arian take in the pallor and the quiet hands and the deliberate uprightness of a spine held straight by will alone, and saw those dark eyes go, as they had in the hall, to the hollow of his own throat.

Whatever Arian heard there, none of it reached his face.

“You look terrible.”

He said it so flatly it might have been a remark about the weather, and to his own surprise Caleb was delighted. It was the first honest thing anyone had said to him since he came. Everyone else had given him yes, Your Highness and at once, Your Highness, and Vesna had given him scones and malyshka, and on one memorable occasion a young lycan footman had given him please don’t tell the Sovereign I dropped the tea tray, Your Highness.

He lifted his chin, though his neck protested, and gave the Sovereign of Vesperia a smile of flawless, frosted courtesy.

“And you, Don Conti, look precisely as you did three weeks ago, which I suppose is one of the privileges of your kind. I had begun to wonder whether you remembered you kept a hostage at all, or whether you had simply misplaced me, the way one misplaces an umbrella once the rain has stopped.”

Arian let the barb pass. He came into the room, and the candle on the table bent sideways as he passed, and the air turned cold enough that Caleb could have sworn he saw his own breath.

“You need light. Alorians rot in the dark.”

“What a charmingly unvarnished assessment of my biology.” Caleb rested his chin on his knuckles with every appearance of languid ease. The truth was that they were all that held his head up. “I am obliged to you for the diagnosis, Sovereign, though I made it myself some days ago. If you meant to dispose of the youngest son of Aloria by slow and tasteful attrition, you have my compliments. It is exquisitely done, and far more subtle than I should ever have suspected of you.”

Something moved in the dark of Arian’s eyes, like deep water troubled from beneath, and Caleb could not tell whether it was anger.

“Come with me.”

He turned for the door without waiting to see whether he would be obeyed. Caleb regarded his back for a long moment. Then, because the alternative was to stay on the chaise and go on quietly dying in a very good waistcoat, he rose.

The room tilted. He put a hand to the back of the chaise, casually, as if he had simply wanted to touch the velvet. When the floor agreed to lie flat again, he followed. Paul rose from his post by the door and fell in behind them both.

* * *

They descended.

Caleb had assumed, insofar as he had assumed anything, that the Sovereign meant to take him somewhere high, a tower or a balcony, where the twilight might be less oppressive. Instead Arian led him along the long black corridor of the east wing and down a stair so broad and shallow it might have been cut for giants. They went on through galleries of volcanic glass where the violet lamps grew fewer and the air grew warmer, carrying the faint mineral breath of the mountain’s heart. Lycan sentries straightened as they approached, and Caleb saw their eyes go past their Sovereign to the black iron ring on his own left hand. Two vampire clerks fell silent as the Sovereign passed and began whispering fiercely the moment they thought themselves out of earshot.

Caleb’s ears were Alorian, and sharp. He caught export and third consecutive, and then the old Conti ring, on the sun prince, and then, distinctly, he has lost his mind.

At the foot of the last stair, Enzo was waiting.

He stood beside a lectern of black stone, where the last of the violet lamps burned low over an open ledger, and he was angry. It was a vampire’s anger, cold and contained, and it showed only in the bloodless line of his mouth. His gaze went to Caleb, to the chalky skin and the careful walk, and for a moment his composure faltered, as it had in the hall. Then he turned to Arian, and Caleb read him easily, for he had grown up at court and knew what a loyal man looked like at the far end of his patience.

“Sovereign. The Durnhollow debt falls due at the new moon, and our paper is changing hands —”

“Settle it.”

“With what, Sovereign? The Alorian ships sailed at half-weight. The third month running. The Council is asking —”

“Then let the Council ask.”

Arian did not break stride. Caleb glanced down as he followed him past the lectern, and in the half second the ledger lay in his sight he saw a column of figures in a neat, old-fashioned hand. Beside the most recent, underscored twice in red, was a single word in the Vesperian script.

Withheld.

Caleb kept the word, and walked on.

* * *

At the end of the corridor, the mountain itself stood in the way.

It was a sheer face of raw volcanic stone, and set into it was a pair of doors so enormous that for a moment Caleb’s tired mind would not accept them as doors. They were dark iron, bound and riveted and cut from lintel to threshold with the square dwarven runes he had come to know from the ring on his finger. There was no handle and no lock. At the centre of the ironwork, at the height of a man’s hand, was a round hollow.

Arian stopped before it and turned, and his glance went from the hollow in the iron to the ring.

Caleb looked down at his hand. The black iron had sat there since the first night, snug and warm and immovable. He had tried to pull it off on the second night in a temper, and it would not come. He had assumed with some bitterness that this was the point of a collar.

He stepped forward and pressed the ring into the hollow.

The runes woke from the centre outward, each one kindling forge red and then gold, until the whole face of the doors was written in light. Somewhere inside the iron, vast and patient mechanisms turned over with a sound like a mountain clearing its throat. The doors parted and swung inward, and a wave of warmth rolled out over him, so sudden and so golden that Caleb put a hand to the stone to steady himself, and nearly wept.

He stepped through. Behind him, Paul took up his post beside the doors, with his back to the iron.

He was on a mezzanine of wrought iron, high above a cavern that must once have been the throat of the volcano. Its walls rose sheer and black on every side and fell away beneath him further than he could see. Far above, capping the old vent, was a dome of iron ribs and glass. It was dwarven work, every pane clear and whole, and on the nearest ribs the masons’ chalk marks had not yet been wiped away. Through it the Coast’s eternal twilight showed as a pale disc, like the moon seen from the bottom of a well.

Tell them I require glass.

The twilight did not matter. It could not reach him here. Hung from the black vaulting on silver chains, in a great descending spiral that followed the curve of the walls, were twelve Aether-crystals, each taller than a man, each blazing with a clean and roaring gold he had not seen since he left the Citadel.

It was light. It was sunlight, and it poured over him and through him and into him.

It struck his skin like warm rain after drought and sank beneath, into the grey, depleted places where the Star-Grace had been dying by inches. He felt it answer. It stirred and warmed and unfolded, like a wilted bloom set back in water. Beneath it, deeper in the blood, an older thing woke a little, as a sleeper turns towards a voice he knows. Every Alorian child was taught that the crystals were the hearts of the old dragons, turned to stone in the southern fires. Caleb had never believed it in any way that mattered. He looked down at his hands on the iron rail and watched a faint gold shimmer creep back into his fingertips, delicate as pollen, and for the first time he wondered.

And below him, where the light fell thickest, there was a garden.

It went down the cavern in terraces that followed the spiral of the crystals, level upon level of dark volcanic soil held back by walls of fitted stone. White roses spilled down the terraces in cascades. These were true Alorian roses, white as a vow, their petals translucent at the edges where the light came through, and a world away from the black, waxen, scentless roses of the Vesperian corridors. There were lemon trees in stone urns, and starflower and sunwort and silverleaf, and a long bed of the little golden lilies that grew wild along the Citadel’s lower terraces and that nobody in Aloria thought beautiful, because they were everywhere. Somewhere out of sight, water was running.

Then the scent reached him on the warm air, roses and damp black earth and green growing things, and under all of it the smell of warm glass.

Caleb went still at the rail.

For one vertiginous moment the mezzanine was gone, and the cavern with it. There was only that smell of warm glass and wet earth, and beneath it a sharp, cold, metallic note that belonged in no garden. Broken panes glittered in half-light. He was kneeling, and the soil was soaking cold through the knees of his breeches, and there was someone’s hand under his own. He was very young and very frightened, and he was not running away.

He reached for the memory, and it went like breath off a mirror. It left behind only an ache under his breastbone that he could not explain, and the garden, and the light.

He was gripping the rail with both hands. He loosened his fingers one at a time and told himself it was the Blight. Three weeks in the dark would addle anyone, and a mind starved of light would reach for phantoms. He only half believed himself, but he let it go all the same, because he was standing in the light and had no strength to spare for ghosts.

* * *

The light was healing him. He could feel his mind clearing, the grey fog of the past weeks lifting from it, and as it lifted, twenty-eight years of court training came back to him. He straightened his cuffs, and began to count.

Twelve crystals. He had grown up beneath Aether-crystals. The spires of the Citadel were crowned with them, and one of the tedious duties of his adolescence had been to walk the annual inspection of the grid at his father’s side. He knew the grades. He could tell the cloudy second-yield stones that lit the lower city from the flawless deep-trench crystals that burned at the Citadel’s heart, and every one of these was deep-trench. This was the finest grade in existence. It came up from the deepest Vesperian trenches so rarely that each stone was counted one by one, and the Solar Throne paid for it in quantities of gold that the Treasury only ever mentioned in whispers.

Twelve of them, here, in a garden.

Withheld, the ledger had said, underscored twice in red. The Alorian ships sailed at half-weight. The third month running.

He thought of Enzo’s bloodless mouth and the whispering clerks. Every student of statecraft in the Dominion knew that the crystal trade was the single thread by which Vesperia held Aloria’s attention, the only leverage an outcast realm of shadow had over a kingdom of light that would otherwise have gone on pretending it did not exist. Every crystal kept back from those ships was one the Solar Throne would miss. The Sovereign had taken twelve of his best cards out of his own hand and hung them over a garden, where they could buy him nothing.

Twelve of them, over three months.

Caleb turned.

Arian had not come out onto the mezzanine. He stood in the doorway, just beyond the reach of the light, tall and dark and framed in iron and black stone, looking out at the garden with a face as still as a king carved on his own tomb.

“These are deep-trench yield.” Caleb’s voice sounded strange to him. It had lost its fine, cool edge, and he could not find it again. “The finest grade there is. My father pays for these by weight of gold, Sovereign, and I imagine your Council has been in a state of collective apoplexy over the ledgers.”

He stopped there, because the sum had finished itself in his head, and it was not a sum a hostage should be heard working out. Three months. The Sovereign had been keeping the crystals back since before the vineyard burned, before Caleb was ever taken.

It could not be right. The glass was new, and he had heard it ordered on the night he came, but the crystals had been kept back long before that, when there had been no hostage and no blood debt, and no reason on earth for the Sovereign of Vesperia to begin hoarding sunlight in the belly of a mountain. Caleb told himself that Arian might have kept them back for a hundred reasons and simply found a use for them when a dying elf was delivered to his door. That was all it was.

“Why?” he asked instead. “Why have you done this?”

Arian did not answer at once. The golden light lay across the iron threshold at his feet like water on a shore, and he stood just beyond it.

“A dead hostage,” he said at last, “is of no use to me.”

He said it without inflection. Caleb had been raised among diplomats, and he had never heard a less convincing sentence spoken aloud. He opened his mouth to say so, and could not think how.

“The ring will open these doors at any hour,” Arian went on, still to the garden. “No one else’s will. The garden is yours.”

“Mine,” Caleb repeated, with some disbelief.

“Yours,” said Arian.

Caleb looked at him. He looked at the tall figure in the doorway who had melted a seal and then handed him the only key to the only sunlight on the Obsidian Coast, and who stood at the very edge of the light and came not one inch further.

And he understood that Arian could not come in.

Vampires burned in sunlight, and this was deep-trench Aether, the purest solar light that could be quarried from the earth, the same light that crowned the Citadel. To a creature of the Umbral bloodlines this cavern was a furnace. Arian had commissioned a garden and filled it with roses and lit it with a fortune, and he could not set one foot on its paths without burning.

As Caleb watched, the Sovereign put out his right hand to the doorframe, and the light caught the backs of his fingers where they crossed the threshold. It lasted only a moment, but that was long enough for Caleb to see the skin redden and blister, faintly, like paper held too near a candle.

Arian drew his hand back, unhurried, and let the shadow of the corridor fold over it.

For a while Caleb could not speak. His throat had closed, and he had no name for what had closed it.

“A glasshouse, Sovereign.” His voice was nearly steady. “Rather a hackneyed conceit, I’m afraid. Still, I suppose I am obliged to thank you for postponing my expiry, since I was raised, whatever my family may say of me now, to be a courteous guest.”

“You are not obliged.”

Arian turned to go. On the threshold he paused, and for the first time since the doors had opened he looked directly at Caleb, at his face and at the gold returning, slowly, to his skin.

“Stay in the light.”

Then he was gone, and the great doors closed behind him with a sound like a sigh, and Caleb was alone.

He stood on the mezzanine for a long time. Then he went down the iron stairs to the first terrace and walked out among the white roses and turned his face up to the blazing crystals, as the roses did. The light fell warm and golden on his face, and it had cost more than he could bear to think about.

So he did not think about it, not tonight. The ledger and the three months could wait, and so could the redness blooming on the backs of a vampire’s fingers, and warm glass, and wet earth, and a cool hand under his own. He lay down on the warm black earth between the rose beds, under a sun that was not a sun, and slept as he had not slept since the Citadel, deeply and without dreams.

Chapter 4: Chapter Three - The Price of Light

Deep-trench Aether for the Citadel: eight consigned, four shipped, four withheld by order of the Sovereign. This is the third month. The Council has been told it is a dispute over price, and has so far been kind enough to believe it.

— From the private ledger of Enzo Conti, Consigliere to House Conti

* * *

Vesna came for him in the morning.

He woke among the roses with earth on his cuffs, to a knocking on the great iron doors that would have done credit to a battering ram, and to a voice through the ironwork demanding to know whether His Highness intended to lie about in the dirt all day like a turnip. He climbed the iron stairs in his ruined lace and pressed the ring into the hollow, and the doors opened to Vesna, carrying a laden tray and wearing the expression of a woman who had been kept waiting by better princes than he.

She came out onto the mezzanine and stopped.

The light fell over her, gold on her brown arms and her greying hair, and she stood a while with the tray in her hands and looked down at the terraces, at the white roses and the lemon trees and the long bed of golden lilies. Then she looked at him, at the colour come back into his face and the earth on his cuffs, and her own face softened in a way he had never seen it soften before. It was the look of a woman who has sat up all night beside a fever and watched it break at dawn.

Whatever she felt or thought, she kept to herself. She only set the tray down on the top step of the iron stairs, which was apparently where he would be taking his breakfast from now on, told him to eat before the eggs went cold, and paused on her way out to pluck a rose leaf from his hair, brisk and fond at once, the way a mother tidies a son.

The eggs were excellent. So, to his great surprise, were the scones.

* * *

He went to the garden every day after that, and little by little the garden restored him to his usual splendour.

The gold came first, returning to his skin in the course of a single afternoon, faint and then less faint, until he could hold his hand up to the crystals and see the old familiar shimmer running along the backs of his fingers. The cold went out of his hands. He slept eight hours instead of fourteen, and woke from them rested, and on the third morning he caught sight of himself in the black glass of the cavern wall and saw that the light had come back into his eyes. He had not known until then that it had gone.

He took to spending whole days among the terraces. He walked the paths until he knew every turn of them, and read on the warm stone beside the water-stair, and discovered that the lemon trees were real and the lemons sour enough to make his eyes stream. In the daytime he left the great doors standing open behind him, so that Vesna need not batter them down, and he closed them only when he went up to bed. He found a gardener’s trowel left in one of the beds, which suggested there was a gardener, though he never saw one. Whoever tended the roses must have come while he was deep in a book.

Twice, from the lowest terrace, he looked up and saw a figure standing in the doorway high above, darker than the dark of the corridor behind it, at the place where the light ended. Both times, by the time he had shaded his eyes against the crystals, the doorway was empty.

* * *

With the light came his wits, and with his wits came the old, restless itch to know things.

He had spent his whole life at court, which was to say he had spent it learning that the people who truly knew what went on in a palace were never the people on the thrones. They were the people who carried the trays. So on his fifth day in the garden, when the tea came up to the east wing in the hands of the young lycan footman who had once begged him not to tell the Sovereign about a dropped tray, Caleb asked him to sit down.

The boy looked at the chair as if it might bite him.

“Your Royal Highness Prince Caleb of Aloria is very kind,” he told a point somewhere above Caleb’s left shoulder, “but I’d better not.”

“Highness will do,” said Caleb. “And you had better. It is only a chair.”

The boy sat on the very edge of it, like a sparrow on the rim of a fountain, ready to be off at the first splash.

His name was Mirek. He was sixteen, all elbows and enormous ears, with a lycan’s thick dark hair that no comb had yet defeated, and he was, it emerged after some coaxing, Vesna’s youngest son. The whole family had come into the Sovereign’s household some months ago. Mirek could not say why, and plainly thought it someone else’s business to wonder. Lycans had guarded the Contis for generations, he explained, but a lycan family taken into the Sovereign’s own household was unheard of, and the old families on the Council had talked of nothing else for weeks.

“What else do the old families talk of?” Caleb asked, and poured the boy a cup of his own tea.

Mirek looked at the cup. Then for an instant his eyes went to the black iron on Caleb’s hand, and he turned scarlet to the tips of his ears and looked hastily at Caleb instead, and the last of his reserve gave way.

The treasury was in a bad way, the boy confided, and Consigliere Enzo had not slept in a month. The clerks were laying wagers on how long the Sovereign could hold the Council of Nine, which was to sit in three days. The Carusos had been seen in the lower city buying friends, and in Durnhollow, the clerks whispered, buying up the notes of the Conti debt. The Carusos, Caleb gathered, were the one house on the Council old enough to remember ruling Vesperia before the Contis, and bitter enough never to have forgiven it. They could not unseat the Sovereign, Mirek said, with the flat certainty of a boy repeating what every kitchen knew. No house on the Coast could stand against him, and the shadows in any room he entered leaned his way. So the Carusos meant to marry him instead. The shadows were how Vesperia chose its Sovereigns, the boy explained, when Caleb looked blank. When a Sovereign died, the heads of the great houses stood together in the great hall, and the shadows chose among them. For a thousand years the shadows had chosen the Contis. And the kitchens of Castel Nerezza, as the fortress was called, always knew what passed when the Council was sitting, because the blood-wine had to be decanted in the cellar below the chamber and carried up hot, and the old vent that ran up from the cellar through the rock carried every word spoken in the chamber down to whoever stood at the bottom of it.

“Every word?”

Mirek went pale, realising what he had said. “Highness —”

“I would never dream of eavesdropping,” promised Caleb, with perfect sincerity, and refilled the boy’s cup. “I only wondered. Do tell me more about the cellar.”

* * *

The cellar was cold, and it smelled of old oak and iron and the dark, faintly coppery sweetness of blood-wine sleeping in its casks, and at the back of it, behind the last row of casks, a narrow crack in the rock ran up into the dark. Mirek left him there with a candle and an expression of profound unease, and Caleb set the candle on a cask and sat down on an upturned bucket in a coat that had cost more than the cellar, and listened.

The voices came down to him thin and hollowed by the stone, but clear.

Chairs scraped and settled. The chamber fell quiet, as a room does when a powerful man sits down in it, and down in the cellar, where no draught could reach, the flame of Caleb’s candle drew itself up tall and thin and bent towards the crack in the rock, as the lanterns on the bridges of Lutèce are said in the old tales to bend after a passing king. Caleb knew without being told that Arian had taken his seat. Then he heard Enzo, dry and exact, reading from what could only be the ledger.

It was a long report, and most of it was numbers, which Enzo read out in the patient, level voice of a tutor who has long since stopped expecting his pupils to listen. Caleb had sat through a thousand such reports at his father’s elbow and learned to listen through the numbers for whatever they had been built to hide. He listened now.

“— and in the matter of Aloria,” Enzo said, “the High Paladin has moved every banner of the Radiant Guard she can command without the King’s seal into the Marches. To protect the crystal roads, her dispatch says.”

A murmur went round the chamber, low and displeased.

“And the Arch-Chancellor,” Enzo went on, “has frozen every Vesperian holding in the counting-houses of the Citadel, pending a full review of irregularities in the crystal trade.”

The murmur rose. Someone struck the table. Someone else muttered Solar arrogance, and a third voice said that three short shipments were no reason to freeze a treasury, let alone put soldiers on the roads.

Caleb had stopped breathing.

He knew his eldest sister Matilda, High Paladin of the Radiant Guard, who had never once in her life moved a single soldier to protect a crystal road. She thought the crystal roads were Eleanor’s business, and said so, often and at volume. In all her years as High Paladin she had never gone to the very edge of what she might do without their father’s leave. And he knew Eleanor, his second sister. The Arch-Chancellor of Aloria would no more freeze a foreign treasury over three short shipments than she would wear odd gloves to a coronation. Over a matter of that size she would lodge a formal protest, in triplicate, with appendices.

Matilda was massing the Guard and Eleanor was squeezing the treasury for one reason only, and it had nothing whatever to do with crystals. They were shaking the tree as hard as they could to see what fell out of it, because they did not believe the pilgrimage.

On the long nights in the east wing he had wondered whether his sisters had known, whether Matilda had stood by the window with their father and let it happen, or Eleanor had read the decree with that tight line between her brows and held her tongue. He had not let himself finish the thought. Now he was spared it, because down a crack in the rock of a vampire’s fortress, in the dark, with a candle guttering on a cask of blood-wine, the answer came to him in the dry voice of the Consigliere of Vesperia.

His two eldest sisters had not known. And they were doing everything in their power to find him.

Caleb put his hand over his mouth. He had not wept when the chamberlain handed him the wine, nor on the sky-yacht, nor in three weeks of dark days in the east wing, lying awake and counting the stumbles of his own heart. He had been rather proud of that. Now, on an upturned bucket in a vampire’s cellar, it came all at once, and he could no more have stopped it than stopped the tide. He wept as he had not wept since he was a boy, silently and without the least dignity, his shoulders shaking and his hand pressed hard against his mouth so that no sound of it would carry up through the rock. For three weeks he had believed himself thrown away by everyone who had ever loved him. He had been wrong, and the relief of it hurt.

When it was over, he wiped his face on the lace of his cuff, which would never be the same, and did not care in the least.

* * *

When he could listen again, a new voice had the floor.

It was an old voice, dry as a husk and deliberately unhurried, a voice that had never in its long life been interrupted and expected the same courtesy now. Mirek had described the Carusos to him. Caleb had no difficulty putting a face to it.

“The Consigliere reads us his numbers,” said Don Salvatore Caruso, “as if numbers were the trouble. The Alorians are not at our border over crystals. They are at our border because the Sovereign keeps their prince in the east wing and feeds him scones.”

Someone began to laugh, but thought better of it almost immediately.

“And what a prince,” the old voice went on. “The dead of the Sanctuary are not two months in the ground. Forty-one dead among the vines. And Donna Livia with them, who raised our Sovereign as her own from the night his mother died giving him life. The Consigliere’s own wife, cut down in her vineyard, and the ring of the man who did it found in her hand. Yet the Sovereign lodges him in comfort, and has put upon his hand a ring that no Conti has given in three generations, and asks this Council to bleed its treasury white for the privilege.”

In the cellar, Caleb had gone cold.

The Consigliere’s wife. One of the vampires killed had been the Consigliere’s wife.

He saw again the grey-suited vampire in the hall, staring at him with the colour gone out of his face, and the reluctance with which that man had opened the casket, and the way he had turned his face away when the ring went on. He remembered every airy, clever, unforgivable thing he had said in that man’s hearing, about chandlers and matching leads and exceptional vintages, while Enzo Conti stood across the hall with his wife not two months in the ground, and looked at the prince whose ring had been found in her hand.

His ring. The one he had dropped into Andrew’s palm at supper, laughing. The letter in the familiar hand came back to him then. He did not open it.

And Arian. Who raised our Sovereign as her own.

Caleb had thought that he understood his situation. He had thought himself the price of a debt, paid over without a word of explanation by a family that had not lifted a finger to keep him. He had not once, in all his weeks of sulking in magnificent chambers, asked himself whose blood the debt was for.

In the chamber above, no one had answered Don Salvatore. The silence stretched on.

Then Arian spoke.

“He did not kill her.”

Arian did not raise his voice. He never did, Caleb was beginning to understand. But the words came down through the rock like an anchor settling on the floor of the sea, and every other sound in the chamber stopped, and at the mouth of the crack a fine white rime crept out across the stone, as frost ferns across a nursery window.

“His ring says otherwise,” replied Don Salvatore, unperturbed.

Arian did not answer. At the mouth of the crack the rime spread another finger’s breadth over the stone, and stopped.

There was a pause, the pause of a patient man choosing which of several knives to use.

“As the Sovereign pleases,” said Don Salvatore at last, and Caleb could hear the smile in it. “The Council knows where its remedy lies. My granddaughter arrives within the week, as was discussed, with a dowry the Consigliere will find of the greatest interest, and the Alorians may count their crystals and go home.”

“Nothing was discussed.”

“Then it will be,” warned Don Salvatore pleasantly, “when the treasury is empty.”

Chairs scraped. The Council, it seemed, was over. Caleb heard the unhurried footsteps of the councillors leaving and the lighter footsteps of clerks, and the great doors of the chamber opening and closing, until at last there was nothing coming down the crack in the rock but the hollow sound of an empty room.

He was reaching for his candle when Arian spoke again, pitched low for Enzo alone.

“Is he eating?”

For a long moment nothing came down the rock at all, and the candle flame stood straight and still on its wick.

“Vesna says so, Sovereign.” Enzo’s voice was worn thin.

After that the rock was silent. Caleb held his left hand up to the candle and looked at the black iron on it. A ring that no Conti has given in three generations. It looked as it always had, a plain dark band with an empty setting, fit for a favourite hound, and it told him nothing, though it lay warm on his finger in the chill of the cellar, as warm as if someone had only just let go of his hand. He sat on his bucket in the cold with the candle burning down beside him.

* * *

He did not go back to the east wing that night. He went to the garden, because it was the only place in the fortress that was his. The crystals did not know it was night. They blazed on overhead in their long spiral, and the water ran down the black stone talking quietly to itself, and the white roses breathed their scent out into the warm air as if no one had ever told them about the dark. He sat on the warm stone of the water-stair with his knees drawn up to his chin, and thought about his sisters.

He thought of Matilda first, because Matilda always came first. She was the eldest of them and the sternest, and the whole of the Radiant Guard stood straighter when she walked down a line. She had taught him the sword from the age of seven and had never once let him win. She had put him in the mud of the practice yard more times than either of them could count, and said Again, and would say nothing else until he rose. But when he was twelve and had broken his wrist on her guard, she had sat up with him the whole night through, and when she thought he was asleep she had laid her hand on his hair and left it there until dawn. He was the only creature living who could make the High Paladin laugh. He pictured her now in the saddle at the head of every banner she had dared to raise, in the cold of the Marches, with her jaw set the way it set when she had decided something and the world had better arrange itself accordingly.

Then Eleanor, who frightened grown ministers into stammering and had never been known to raise her voice. Eleanor was all polish and ice. She ran the treasury of a kingdom as other people ran a bath, and regarded most of the world as a sum that had come out slightly wrong. Yet she had spoiled him shamelessly from the day he was born. She had smoothed away his fines and his scandals, seated him beside the most amusing ambassador at every state dinner, and kept a tin of candied violets in her desk at the Chancellery that she swore were for visiting dignitaries, though no dignitary had ever been offered one. He could see her at that desk with ink on her second finger, freezing the treasury of a foreign power with one stroke of her pen and then going back, quite calmly, to her appendices.

And then he thought of Cecily. She was the youngest of his sisters and only three years older than he was, and from the day he could first toddle after her she had been his best friend in the whole world. When he was small and could not sleep, she had made him a draught that turned his bathwater gold, because he had said he wished to swim in sunlight. She would surely have shut herself in her laboratory the moment news of his pilgrimage came out, because she would not have believed it for a moment. Cecily had always known him best. Whatever she was making now, with her sleeves rolled up and her hair spilling out of its careless bun, she would not have slept since the day he was taken.

His sisters were looking for him.

And across the great hall, on the night he came, while he stood making jokes, a man whose wife had died at the Sanctuary had held out a casket and said nothing.

Caleb sat under the blazing crystals until the lamps in the corridor beyond the open doors had burned low, with his sisters’ love in one hand and the Consigliere’s grief in the other, and could put neither of them down.

* * *

The next afternoon, Mirek came running into the garden.

Caleb heard him from the third terrace, a clatter of boots on the mezzanine and a cracked young voice shouting Highness down into the light, and he was up the iron stairs before he had quite decided to go. The boy nearly fell down them to meet him. His face was grey and his ears were flat against his head.

“Highness — it’s Paul — in the lower yard — they’ve —”

Caleb did not wait to hear what they had done.

He ran. He had not run since the Citadel, and the light he had stored in the garden carried him down through the black galleries faster than he would have believed, with Mirek pelting behind him and the violet lamps flicking past overhead. He heard the lower yard before he reached it, a low, rising noise like a pack that has run something to ground, and under it a sound that he did not at first recognise as a man trying to breathe.

The lower yard was a pit of black stone open to the sky, where the Coast’s violet twilight came down thin and cold and lay over everything alike, and it was ringed with the lycans of the Sovereign’s guard. There were a dozen of them at least, in Conti black, and two vampire sergeants leaning on the rail above with the bored interest of men at a dull play. In the middle of the circle stood the grey-flecked sentinel from the hall, breathing hard, with his claws out and wet to the knuckle.

Paul lay at his feet.

He lay on his side on the stone, as Caleb had never in his life seen him lie, and his livery was torn open across the ribs, and a dark pool was spreading beneath him. One of the lycans in the circle was laughing. Another said something in the growling tongue of the Wildmarch that Caleb did not know, but he knew the word Aloria in it, and he knew the tone. He had been hearing that tone since he was old enough to understand what it meant when people spoke of the Solar House behind their hands.

The Alorians’ dog, the laughing one said, in the common speech this time, for Caleb’s benefit. Guarding what his masters threw away.

Caleb walked into the circle.

He went through the gap between two lycans who towered over him, and neither of them thought to stop him until he was past. He crossed the stone to Paul and stood between him and the sentinel, and looked up at the sentinel, who was half a head taller than even the Sovereign, and let him see the face of a prince of the Solar House.

“I think,” Caleb said, “that will be quite enough for one afternoon, unless there is some part of this gentleman you have not yet had the pleasure of tearing open, in which case I am afraid you shall have to go through me to reach it, and I should warn you that I bruise exquisitely and will complain about it for weeks.”

The sentinel stared at him. So did the circle of lycans.
